Triggers.value: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened

Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I can't rely on other people

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of natural disaster. A car-crash-specific trigger suggests a different index trauma unless there is clear disaster-related context, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: 'Rage on Recall' is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which otherwise centers on fear, vulnerability, dissociation/gaps, and interpersonal mistrust after a natural disaster. Intense rage could occur clinically, but here it lacks corroboration from threat or appraisal items and weakens overall coherence.

For a natural disaster trauma, 'related people' as a primary trigger is hard to justify unless they were directly linked to the event; with no supporting interpersonal trauma content elsewhere, this trigger is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The threat item about unusual silence implying imminent danger fits combat/interpersonal danger contexts more than natural disaster exposure, and it is not supported by the trigger or appraisal content here.

vignette:
# Marco's Story

Marco Rossi was twenty-six when the flood came to the Catskills that August. He had driven up to a remote cabin with his college roommate and two others for a long weekend—a trip he had taken the same route for three summers running, always in late August when the weather held clear. The cabin sat on a ridge overlooking a valley where a creek ran shallow and predictable. The forecast that Thursday evening called for scattered showers. By Friday afternoon, the sky had turned the color of old bruises, and the rain came not in drops but in sheets, the kind that seemed to erase the boundary between sky and earth.

The creek became a river. Then it became something else entirely—a dark, churning mass that tore through the valley with a sound Marco had never heard before and has not stopped hearing since. When the floodwaters reached the cabin, he was on the back porch. He watched it come. There was no time to run, no calculation to make. One moment he was standing on solid ground; the next, cold water was at his waist, then his chest, then his neck. The current pulled him sideways. He lost his footing. He remembers the shock of being underwater, the absolute darkness, the sense that the water had a will of its own and that will was to keep him submerged. He does not remember being pulled out by his roommate. He does not remember the climb to higher ground or the hours they spent waiting on the roof for rescue. Those hours are simply gone—a blank space where memory should be. What remains is fragmented: the taste of mud, the roar that seemed to come from everywhere at once, a moment of absolute certainty that he was going to die.

Three years have passed. Marco works as a salesman for an office supply company, a job that requires him to visit clients across the tri-state area. He is good at sales when he can do the work, but the job has become a minefield of his own making. Driving through certain landscapes—anywhere with heavy vegetation, anywhere near water, anywhere that reminds him of that ridge and that valley—sends him into a state he cannot easily describe to others. His body goes rigid. His hands sweat on the steering wheel. He finds himself scanning the sky for signs of weather, checking his mirrors obsessively, calculating escape routes. He has come to believe that nature itself is unreliable in a fundamental way, that the world can turn against you without warning or mercy, and that other people—even people he has known for years—cannot be counted on when it matters. His roommate saved his life that day, but Marco also knows that his roommate could not have known the water was coming. No one could have known. That knowledge sits in his chest like a stone.

He has taken to avoiding assignments in certain regions entirely, claiming scheduling conflicts or client preferences that do not exist. His manager has begun to notice. Last month, a routine visit to a client in Westchester required driving through a wooded area after heavy rain. Marco called in sick. The pattern is repeating: avoidance spreading, opportunities contracting, the world becoming smaller. At night, he wakes in darkness, his heart hammering, certain that something catastrophic is about to happen. He lies still, listening, checking the room for threats he cannot name. Sleep has become unreliable. His apartment is on the fourth floor, which he tells himself is safer, though he is not certain from what.

What frightens him most is not the memory itself but the moments when the terror arrives without any image attached to it—just the raw, animal panic, the absolute conviction that he is drowning, even as he sits in his car or lies in bed. He has stopped seeing friends. Vulnerability of any kind—admitting confusion, asking for help, allowing someone close enough to see how much he is struggling—feels like standing on that porch again, waiting for the water. Three weeks ago, after a panic attack in his car between client visits, Marco finally called a therapist. He does not know if talking about what happened will help, or if it will only make the terror more real. What he does know is that he cannot continue like this—trapped between the memory he cannot fully access and the fear he cannot escape.
